methodological_rigor.justification: The study is a retrospective single-institution cohort of 659 EC patients treated across a very wide window (1989–2022), raising concerns about secular changes in treatment and pathology practice; no power calculation is reported. The AI classifier was trained on only 2235 lymphocytes from 4 cases, with F1 evaluated on just 2 cases — a very small training/validation footprint for the central measurement — and the Results report an ROC AUC of only 0.570 (abstract/text), indicating weak discrimination despite later survival significance. The ROC-derived TIL cut-off was derived in the same cohort used for Kaplan–Meier and Cox analyses, raising optimism/overfitting concerns, though sensitivity analyses across quartile cut-offs and candidate areas (Supporting Information) and AIC/BIC comparison partially mitigate this. Statistical methods (log-rank, Cox with interaction terms, backward stepwise multivariate) are appropriate, but there is no external validation, no correction for multiple sensitivity/subgroup comparisons, and inter-observer reproducibility of the manual invasive-front annotation (acknowledged as a limitation) was not quantified.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an individual retrospective cohort study evaluating a prognostic biomarker (AI-quantified TILs) with PFS and OS as patient-relevant endpoints, mapping to Oxford LoE 2b. Clinical relevance is plausible: AI quantification could standardize TIL assessment and inform EC risk stratification alongside MMR/POLE, and multivariate HRs for PFS (0.61) and OS (0.54) are clinically meaningful. However, the ROC AUC of 0.57 for recurrence, lack of external validation, and absence of integration with molecular classifiers (POLE untested) make the translational path aspirational rather than practice-ready. The findings are therefore a plausible but not yet demonstrated step toward a deployable prognostic tool.

reporting_quality.justification: REMARK applies as this is a prognostic biomarker study; STROBE elements also apply given the retrospective cohort design. Inclusion/exclusion, assay description, cut-off derivation, Cox modeling, and prespecified subgroup/sensitivity analyses are reported, but several REMARK items are incomplete: no CONSORT-style patient-flow diagram, no formal handling of missing data, no external validation, and no reporting of the full distribution of adjuvant treatments or follow-up completeness. Data and code availability are not described in the retained text — the AI classifier, trained weights, annotations, and raw lymphocyte counts are not stated as deposited — so reproducibility rests only on the written methods, warranting a low data-availability score.

novelty_literature.justification: The conceptual novelty is modest: AI-based lymphocyte detection on H&E has been applied to multiple tumor types including a directly analogous pipeline in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (ref 23) and lymphocyte detection networks in other cancers (refs 28–30). The specific contribution is extending an off-the-shelf HALO/Object Phenotyper classifier to endometrial carcinoma and defining a 500-μm band straddling the invasive front — an incremental methodological variation rather than a new model or mechanism. Prior non-AI TIL prognostic work in EC is extensive (refs 13–16, 31–34, 42), so the empirical finding (High-TIL predicts better PFS/OS) confirms rather than challenges existing knowledge. The authors appropriately position the gap but do not demonstrate a genuinely new capability beyond automation.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is organized conventionally with a clear abstract that is quantitatively grounded (HRs with 95% CIs, p-values, group sizes) and accurately reflects the paper. Methods are generally detailed, though the invasive-frontline annotation and classifier training description would benefit from clarification about who annotated and how reproducibility was assessed. The Discussion limitations section is unusually long and runs together many distinct limitations into a single dense paragraph that would read better as structured subpoints. Figure captions are informative, but there is a numerical inconsistency between the abstract/text (AUC 0.570) and Figure 4 caption (AUC 0.573) that should be reconciled.

key_strengths: Large single-institution cohort of 659 EC patients with long follow-up (median 63 months) and relevant endpoints (PFS, OS)
Pre-specified sensitivity analyses across candidate TIL evaluation areas and alternative cut-offs with AIC/BIC comparison
Multivariate Cox models with interaction terms for MMR status and subgroup analyses by histology and MMR status
F1 score (0.81) for lymphocyte detection within the range reported in prior AI-TIL literature
key_concerns: ROC AUC for recurrence of only 0.570 indicates weak discrimination; cut-off derived in the same cohort used for survival inference risks optimism
AI classifier trained on only 4 cases/2235 lymphocytes and F1 evaluated on 2 cases — very small training/validation footprint not stratified by histological subtype
No external validation cohort and no orthogonal (molecular/transcriptomic) validation; POLE status not assessed
Single-institution retrospective design spanning 1989–2022 with no reporting on secular treatment heterogeneity or missing data handling
Novelty is incremental — extends an existing AI TIL pipeline (ovarian HGSC analog) to EC without a new method or mechanism
Data/code availability not addressed; manual invasive-front annotation reproducibility not quantified
chief_reviewer.rationale: A competently executed but incremental single-center retrospective prognostic biomarker study with weak classifier discrimination (AUC 0.57), internal cut-off derivation, and no external validation; appropriate for a Tier 3 oncology journal after major revisions addressing validation, cut-off robustness, and reporting completeness.
